title: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Strength as a supposed selective factor”. Scope: Foraminifera

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-12: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The survival prediction is measurable, but existing public records mainly concern preserved shells rather than individual breakage hazards and fitness. A convincing causal test would require new mechanical and ecological measurements.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate measured shell strength and damage frequency to survival, reproduction and lineage persistence across environments, controlling for size and habitat. A positive fitness effect of strength or frequent lethal breakage would refute the claim; negligible effects in adequately powered samples would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Absence of an effect is difficult to establish.

Postmortem fragmentation is confounded with lethal damage.

Open datasets rarely link mechanical strength, breakage and fitness for the same populations.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Death assemblages show that fragile tests are routinely preserved, which speaks to Thompson's observation that breakage is not universal. They do not record the selective gradient of strength, and fragment counts are not a standard open variable across the global census. A comparative test can bound how common destruction is, while the evolutionary claim about strength as a guiding advantage stays weakly identified.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare fragment proportions and shell thickness across assemblages, and test whether more robust forms have higher relative abundance or longer stratigraphic durations. The claim is favored if delicate tests dominate death assemblages with little fragmentation and robustness does not predict persistence; a consistent association of breakage with loss of fragile forms would favor the selective account Thompson rejects.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Abundance of delicate species does not measure whether strength differences affect survival.

Fragments in sediment mix predation, dissolution, compaction, and processing damage.
